overview:
Bhadrabahu migration traditions refer to a cluster of Jain narratives, inscriptions, and later literary retellings that describe a southward movement of Jain monks and laity from the Gangetic heartland to the Deccan, especially to Shravanabelagola in present‑day Karnataka, under the leadership of Ācārya Bhadrabāhu. In these traditions, Bhadrabāhu is portrayed as the last Śruta‑kevalin—an ascetic who possessed complete mastery of the fourteen Pūrvas—and as a pivotal organizer of the Jain saṅgha during a time of crisis. The migration is usually linked to a twelve‑year famine in northern India, which Bhadrabāhu is said to have foreseen or prophesied, prompting him to lead a group of monks southward to safeguard the continuity of Jain practice and scripture.

A central motif in these accounts is the association of Bhadrabāhu with Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Maurya Empire. Digambara‑leaning narratives, supported by local tradition at Shravanabelagola and medieval Jain texts, describe Chandragupta as renouncing his throne, becoming Bhadrabāhu’s disciple, and accompanying him on the migration. At Shravanabelagola, Bhadrabāhu is said to have spent his final years in a cave on Chandragiri hill, where engraved footprints (pādukās) are still venerated. Chandragupta, according to these stories, remained there as an ascetic, worshipping his teacher’s footprints and eventually undertaking sallekhana, the Jain fast unto death. Epigraphic and local heritage materials from Shravanabelagola preserve this tradition and connect it to the broader history of Jain presence in Karnataka.

From a historical‑critical perspective, Bhadrabahu migration traditions sit at the intersection of sectarian memory, regional identity, and the gradual differentiation of Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities. The idea that a major famine led to a southward movement of monks helps explain, in traditional narratives, why certain lineages and textual recensions came to be associated with southern regions, while others remained in the north. Some modern scholars have suggested that the migration story functions as a retrospective explanation for doctrinal and disciplinary differences that later crystallized into distinct sects, rather than a strictly datable event. The chronology of Bhadrabāhu himself, and his precise relationship to Chandragupta Maurya, remains debated; while Jain sources and Shravanabelagola inscriptions affirm the connection, non‑Jain contemporary evidence is lacking, and some historians argue that Bhadrabāhu may be later than Chandragupta or that the emperor’s conversion is a hagiographic development.

Within Jain communities, however, the migration traditions carry more than historical interest. They frame Bhadrabāhu as a model of foresight, renunciation, and scriptural guardianship, and they embed Shravanabelagola and the wider Karnataka region into the sacred geography of Jainism. The cave associated with Bhadrabāhu, the basadis on Chandragiri, and the inscriptions that mention famine and movement of ascetics are woven into pilgrimage practice and local storytelling. These traditions also highlight the resilience of the Jain saṅgha in the face of environmental and political change, presenting migration not as mere displacement but as a deliberate spiritual strategy to preserve non‑violence, austerity, and learning.

Modern scholarship, drawing on inscriptions, regional histories, and critical readings of medieval Jain texts, tends to treat Bhadrabahu migration traditions as layered narratives. At one level, they likely preserve a memory of early Jain expansion into the Deccan and the establishment of monastic centers in Karnataka. At another level, they reflect the theological and sectarian concerns of the communities that transmitted them, including the desire to link royal renunciation, scriptural mastery, and regional sanctity. For students of Jainism, these traditions invite careful distinction between primary epigraphic evidence, later literary elaboration, and contemporary devotional reception, while still acknowledging the deep formative role they play in Jain historical consciousness.

primary_sources.title: Śravaṇabelagola inscriptions (Bhadrabāhu cave and related epigraphy)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous stone inscriptions; compiled by modern epigraphists
primary_sources.translation: “… the Śruta‑kevalin Bhadrabāhu‑svāmin … on account of a twelve‑year famine … went to the southern region …”
primary_sources.notes: Later inscriptions at Shravanabelagola, especially those associated with Chandragiri and the Bhadrabāhu cave, preserve the tradition that Bhadrabāhu, described as a Śruta‑kevalin, predicted or responded to a twelve‑year famine in the north and led a migration of the Jain community to the south. They also mention his residence and death at Shravanabelagola and the veneration of his footprints. These inscriptions are among the earliest material witnesses to the migration narrative and anchor it in a specific sacred landscape, though they are themselves several centuries later than the events they describe.

primary_sources.title: Bhṛhatkathākośa
primary_sources.author: Haribhadra (Śvetāmbara tradition, 10th century CE)
primary_sources.original_text: bhadrabāhuḥ śrutakevalī mahānācāryaḥ… chandragupte mahīpāle saṃnyāsaṃ kārayitvā dakṣiṇāpathaṃ yayau…
primary_sources.transliteration: bhadrabāhuḥ śrutakevalī mahānācāryaḥ… chandragupte mahīpāle saṃnyāsaṃ kārayitvā dakṣiṇāpathaṃ yayau…
primary_sources.translation: “Bhadrabāhu, the Śruta‑kevalin and great ācārya… having brought about renunciation in King Chandragupta, went to the southern region…”
primary_sources.notes: The Bhṛhatkathākośa, a Sanskrit narrative compendium, includes episodes that link Bhadrabāhu with Chandragupta Maurya and a journey to the south. While composed many centuries after the Mauryan period, it reflects a Śvetāmbara reception of the migration tradition and emphasizes Bhadrabāhu’s status as Śruta‑kevalin and spiritual guide. The text blends didactic storytelling with historical memory, and its account must be read critically alongside epigraphic evidence and other Jain sources.

primary_sources.title: Bhadrabāhu‑caritra
primary_sources.author: Anonymous or regional Jain author (likely 15th century CE)
primary_sources.original_text: ujjayinyāṃ bhadrabāhuḥ śrutakevalī dvādaśa‑varṣa‑durbhikṣaṃ vyākhyāya… saṅghaṃ dakṣiṇāpathaṃ nītavān… chandragupte ca rājāne saṃnyāsena saha śravaṇabelagolaṃ prāpayat…
primary_sources.transliteration: ujjayinyāṃ bhadrabāhuḥ śrutakevalī dvādaśa‑varṣa‑durbhikṣaṃ vyākhyāya… saṅghaṃ dakṣiṇāpathaṃ nītavān… chandragupte ca rājāne saṃnyāsena saha śravaṇabelagolaṃ prāpayat…
primary_sources.translation: “At Ujjain, Bhadrabāhu, the Śruta‑kevalin, having foretold a twelve‑year famine… led the community to the southern region… and brought King Chandragupta, together with his renunciation, to Shravanabelagola…”
primary_sources.notes: Bhadrabāhu‑caritra is a later Sanskrit hagiographic work that elaborates the migration story in detail, including Bhadrabāhu’s prophecy at Ujjain, the organized movement of monks and lay followers, and Chandragupta’s renunciation and journey to Shravanabelagola. It is important for understanding how the tradition developed in medieval Jain circles, but its distance from the purported events and its devotional tone mean that historians treat it as a secondary witness, to be compared with inscriptions and earlier narrative sources.

primary_sources.title: Munivaṃśābhyudaya
primary_sources.author: Gunabhadra or Devachandra (Kannada Jain author, c. 17th century CE)
primary_sources.original_text: bhadrabāhu muniya dvādaśa varṣada duṣkāla bhaviyeṃdu heḷi… śravaṇabelagolakke saṅghavannu kāṇḍu hoḷeyalu… chandragupte rājanu tyāga māḍi tapasviyāgi alli sallekhaṇeya mūlake dehavan biṭṭanu…
primary_sources.transliteration: bhadrabāhu muniya dvādaśa varṣada duṣkāla bhaviyeṃdu heḷi… śravaṇabelagolakke saṅghavannu kāṇḍu hoḷeyalu… chandragupte rājanu tyāga māḍi tapasviyāgi alli sallekhaṇeya mūlake dehavan biṭṭanu…
primary_sources.translation: “The monk Bhadrabāhu, saying that a twelve‑year famine would occur… led the community to Shravanabelagola to protect it… King Chandragupta, having renounced, became an ascetic there and abandoned his body through sallekhana…”
primary_sources.notes: This Kannada work, part of a regional Jain literary tradition, reinforces the migration narrative in the vernacular, connecting Bhadrabāhu’s foresight, the movement of the saṅgha, and Chandragupta’s sallekhana at Shravanabelagola. It is valuable for understanding how the story was localized in Karnataka and integrated into the cultural memory of Jain communities there. As with other medieval sources, it is not a contemporary record of Mauryan events but a later articulation of a long‑standing tradition.

primary_sources.title: Pariśiṣṭaparvan (also known as Sthavirāvalī‑caritra)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandra (Śvetāmbara polymath, 12th century CE)
primary_sources.original_text: bhadrabāhuḥ śrutakevalī… chandragupte mahīpāle saṃnyāsaṃ kṛtvā… dakṣiṇāpathaṃ yayau… tatra śravaṇabelagole sallekhanayā deham utsasarja…
primary_sources.transliteration: bhadrabāhuḥ śrutakevalī… chandragupte mahīpāle saṃnyāsaṃ kṛtvā… dakṣiṇāpathaṃ yayau… tatra śravaṇabelagole sallekhanayā deham utsasarja…
primary_sources.translation: “Bhadrabāhu, the Śruta‑kevalin… having brought King Chandragupta to renunciation… went to the southern region… there, at Shravanabelagola, he abandoned his body through sallekhana…”
primary_sources.notes: Hemacandra’s Pariśiṣṭaparvan, a Sanskrit poem that supplements his larger historical‑religious works, includes an influential version of the Bhadrabāhu–Chandragupta story. It presents Bhadrabāhu as the last Śruta‑kevalin and narrates the emperor’s renunciation and journey south. Although composed in the 12th century, it has shaped both Śvetāmbara and broader Jain understandings of the migration and is often cited in discussions of Jain influence on the Mauryan court. Modern historians note its literary and didactic character and use it cautiously as a source for reconstructing early Jain history.

misconceptions.myth: The Bhadrabāhu migration is a fully documented historical event with precise dates and unanimous scholarly agreement.
misconceptions.reality: While Jain inscriptions and medieval texts preserve a strong tradition of Bhadrabāhu leading a migration to Shravanabelagola during a twelve‑year famine, the exact chronology, scale, and details of the event are not securely established by contemporary non‑Jain sources. Modern historians treat the migration story as a layered narrative that likely reflects real patterns of Jain expansion into the Deccan, but they also highlight chronological tensions and the absence of independent corroboration for some elements, such as the precise dating of Bhadrabāhu and his direct association with Chandragupta Maurya.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain sects interpret Bhadrabāhu migration traditions in exactly the same way and see them as the single cause of the Digambara–Śvetāmbara split.
misconceptions.reality: Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions honor Bhadrabāhu as a Śruta‑kevalin and preserve migration narratives, but they differ in details about his role, attire, and textual legacy. Moreover, the divergence between Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities developed over several centuries and involved doctrinal, disciplinary, and regional factors. The migration traditions are one important strand in explaining later differences, not a simple, single cause of sectarian division.

misconceptions.myth: Chandragupta Maurya’s conversion to Jainism and his sallekhana at Shravanabelagola are established facts accepted by all historians.
misconceptions.reality: Jain sources and Shravanabelagola traditions strongly affirm that Chandragupta became Bhadrabāhu’s disciple, migrated south, and undertook sallekhana. However, contemporary non‑Jain evidence for this conversion and death‑rite is lacking, and some scholars argue that these elements are hagiographic, developed in medieval Jain literature to express ideals of royal renunciation. The association remains central in Jain memory and pilgrimage, but it is debated in academic historiography.

misconceptions.myth: Bhadrabāhu migration traditions are purely legendary and have no historical value for understanding Jain presence in South India.
misconceptions.reality: Even though the narratives are shaped by hagiography and sectarian concerns, they are anchored by inscriptions and archaeological evidence that attest to early Jain activity in Karnataka and Shravanabelagola. The migration traditions help explain how Jain communities themselves understood and remembered their movement into the Deccan, and they provide clues about the timing and nature of that expansion, when read critically alongside material and comparative historical data.
